**COASTAL TANK INSPECTION SERVICES, LLC** 310 Veterans Memorial Blvd, Suite 140 Metairie, LA 70005

**[API 653 EXTERNAL INSPECTION REPORT]{.underline}**

**[ABOVEGROUND STORAGE TANK NO. 7]{.underline}**

**Report Number:** CTIS-2023-0612-GF07

**Date of Inspection:** June 12, 2023

**Date of Report:** June 19, 2023

**Client:** Greenfield Specialty Chemicals, Inc.

**Facility:** Plaquemines Parish Manufacturing Facility 2750 Industrial Canal Road Belle Chasse, LA 70037

**Prepared by:** Marcus J. Hebert API 653 Certified Inspector Certification No. 48172

**Reviewed by:** Linda Tran Senior Inspector / Quality Assurance Manager

**Coastal Tank Inspection Services, LLC** 310 Veterans Memorial Blvd, Suite 140 Metairie, LA 70005 Tel: (504) 833-4100

Email: inspections@coastaltank.com

This report is the property of Coastal Tank Inspection Services, LLC and is provided for the exclusive use of the named client. Reproduction or distribution without written authorization is prohibited.

**[Section 1: Executive Summary]{.underline}**

Coastal Tank Inspection Services, LLC (\"CTIS\") was retained by Greenfield Specialty Chemicals, Inc. (\"Greenfield\" or \"Client\") to perform a routine scheduled external inspection of Aboveground Storage Tank No. 7 (\"Tank 7\") at the Plaquemines Parish Manufacturing Facility, located at 2750 Industrial Canal Road, Belle Chasse, Louisiana 70037. The inspection was performed in accordance with the requirements of API Standard 653, *Tank Inspection, Repair, Alteration, and Reconstruction*, Fifth Edition (November 2014, Addendum 2 --- April 2020).

The inspection was performed on June 12, 2023. **This inspection was an external visual inspection only.** Tank 7 was in service and contained product (methyldiethanolamine, \"MDEA\") at the time of inspection. An internal inspection was not performed during this engagement and was not due under the applicable API 653 inspection schedule maintained by the facility. The most recent internal inspection of Tank 7 was completed in March 2019 by CTIS; based on corrosion rate calculations and remaining shell and bottom thickness data obtained during that internal inspection, the next scheduled internal inspection for Tank 7 is not due until approximately 2028--2029, which falls within the standard API 653 internal inspection interval for tanks rated in satisfactory condition.

**Overall Shell Condition Rating: Satisfactory.**

One observation was noted during this inspection: minor surface corrosion was observed at the base ring exterior, concentrated in the south-southeast quadrant of the shell-to-bottom junction. The corrosion is superficial in nature, affecting the exterior coating and the outer surface of the base ring plate. No weeping, seepage, product staining, measurable wall loss, or evidence of through-wall corrosion was observed. The recommendation is to recoat the affected area and continue monitoring at the next scheduled external inspection.

No conditions were observed during this inspection requiring immediate corrective action, removal of the tank from service, or out-of-service designation.

The next scheduled external inspection for Tank 7, based on the 24-month inspection interval established in the facility\'s API 653 inspection program, is June 2025.

**[Section 2: Tank Identification and Specifications]{.underline}**

  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Parameter**                                  **Detail**
  ---------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Tank Designation**                           Tank No. 7 (\"Tank 7\")

  **Location**                                   Tank Farm Area, Plaquemines Parish Manufacturing Facility, 2750 Industrial Canal Road, Belle Chasse, LA 70037

  **Tank Type**                                  Vertical, cylindrical, aboveground storage tank (AST)

  **Construction Material**                      Carbon steel --- ASTM A36 shell plates; ASTM A283 Grade C bottom plates

  **Design Standard**                            API 650, *Welded Tanks for Oil Storage*

  **Nominal Capacity**                           50,000 gallons

  **Diameter**                                   Approximately 12 feet

  **Height**                                     Approximately 20 feet

  **Number of Shell Courses**                    4

  **Year of Construction**                       2011

  **Contents at Time of Inspection**             Methyldiethanolamine (\"MDEA\") --- liquid amine used in gas sweetening processes

  **Approximate Volume at Time of Inspection**   42,000 gallons

  **Foundation Type**                            Concrete ring wall with compacted sand/gravel fill

  **Roof Type**                                  Cone roof, fixed

  **Cathodic Protection**                        External impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP) system installed on tank bottom

  **Secondary Containment**                      Concrete dike containment area (shared with Tank 6)
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Previous Inspections Referenced:**

> • Most recent external inspection: June 2021 (CTIS Report No. CTIS-2021-0608-GF07) --- 24-month cycle
>
> • Most recent internal inspection: March 2019 (CTIS Report No. CTIS-2019-0314-GF07)

**Adjacent Equipment Noted:**

Tank 6 (25,000-gallon monoethanolamine storage tank) is located approximately 20 feet to the northwest within the shared secondary containment area. An electrical junction box is located approximately 15 feet east of the Tank 7 base. A pipe rack connecting the tank farm to the main processing building runs along the northern boundary of the containment area.

**[Section 3: Scope of Inspection]{.underline}**

The scope of this inspection was limited to an **external visual inspection only**, conducted from grade level and via ladder access to the tank roof. The inspection was performed in accordance with API 653, Section 6 --- \"Routine In-Service Inspections\" (external). The following components and areas were included within the scope of this inspection:

> • Visual examination of the tank shell exterior, all courses (Course 1 through Course 4)
>
> • Visual examination of the tank bottom/base ring junction (external accessible areas only)
>
> • Visual examination of roof plates, roof-to-shell junction, and roof fittings
>
> • Visual examination of the foundation, ring wall, and settlement indicators
>
> • Examination of tank appurtenances, including nozzles, vents, gauging equipment, manway cover, and overflow piping
>
> • Review of cathodic protection system readings (most recent CP survey data dated February 2023, provided by the facility)
>
> • Visual examination of the secondary containment area, including the concrete dike, liner, and drain valve

**Scope Limitations:**

This inspection was an external visual inspection only. No internal entry was performed. Internal surfaces of the tank shell, bottom plates, and weld seams were not inspected and are not assessed in this report. Tank 7 was in service and contained approximately 42,000 gallons of MDEA at the time of inspection, precluding internal access. Ultrasonic thickness (UT) measurements were not performed during this inspection. UT readings are scheduled in conjunction with the next internal inspection per the facility\'s API 653 inspection plan. No non-destructive examination (NDE) of weld seams was performed during this inspection. Weld seam integrity assessment, including evaluation of shell-to-bottom weld seams, requires internal access and is outside the scope of a routine external inspection conducted under API 653, Section 6.

**[Section 4: Inspection Findings]{.underline}**

**4.1 Shell Condition (External)**

All four shell courses (Course 1 through Course 4) were visually inspected from grade level and via ladder. No significant pitting, buckling, bulging, or deformation was observed on any shell course. The exterior coating system (epoxy-based) was found to be in good condition on the upper shell courses (Courses 2 through 4), with no visible cracking, peeling, or disbondment. Minor coating degradation was observed on the lower portion of Course 1, consistent with the age of the coating system and normal environmental exposure in the Gulf Coast climate. No areas of active corrosion were noted on Courses 2 through 4.

**Overall Shell Rating: Satisfactory.**

No shell repairs are recommended at this time.

**4.2 Base Ring / Shell-to-Bottom Junction (External)**

The exterior of the base ring and the shell-to-bottom junction were visually examined around the full circumference of the tank. The following observation was noted:

**Finding:** Minor surface corrosion was observed at the base ring exterior, concentrated on the south-southeast quadrant of the shell-to-bottom junction, spanning approximately 3 feet of arc length. The corrosion is superficial in nature, affecting the exterior coating and the outer surface of the base ring plate. No measurable wall loss was detected by visual assessment. No weeping, seepage, or product staining was observed at the base ring. No evidence of through-wall corrosion, leakage, or structural compromise at the base ring was observed during this external inspection.

**Recommendation:** Monitor at next scheduled external inspection (June 2025). Recoating of the affected area with a standard epoxy or polyurethane coating system is recommended to arrest surface corrosion progression. Priority: Routine --- complete within 90 days.

**Note:** The internal condition of the shell-to-bottom weld seam at the base ring could not be assessed during this external inspection. Internal weld seam evaluation requires out-of-service internal inspection and is not within the scope of this report.

**4.3 Tank Roof**

Roof plates and the roof-to-shell junction were inspected via ladder access. Minor surface rust was observed on select roof plates, consistent with age and atmospheric exposure. The surface rust is cosmetic in nature and does not present a structural concern. No holes, tears, or excessive thinning was observed. Roof vents and pressure/vacuum relief valves were inspected and found to be operational and unobstructed. The gauging hatch was inspected and found to be in serviceable condition with an intact gasket.

**Rating: Satisfactory.**

**4.4 Foundation and Settlement**

The concrete ring wall was visually inspected around the full circumference. No visible cracking, spalling, or deterioration of the ring wall was observed. Backfill and grading around the tank base appeared stable, with no evidence of erosion or washout. Settlement survey reference points were reviewed against prior survey data. No differential settlement exceeding API 653 limits (1 inch in 10 feet of circumference) was identified.

**Rating: Satisfactory.**

**4.5 Appurtenances.** Tank nozzles, the manway cover, gauging hatch, and overflow line were visually examined. All connections appeared secure and in good condition. Gaskets at the manway cover and flanged nozzle connections were found to be in serviceable condition, with no visible deterioration, hardening, or leakage. The overflow line was clear and properly routed to the secondary containment area.

**Rating: Satisfactory.**

**4.6 Secondary Containment**

The concrete dike and liner forming the secondary containment area (shared with Tank 6) were visually inspected. No cracks, erosion, or deterioration of the containment structure was observed. The containment floor showed no evidence of product staining, discoloration, or accumulation that would indicate a release from Tank 7 or Tank 6. The containment drain valve was in the closed and locked position. Containment capacity was verified as adequate per the facility\'s Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) Plan requirements.

**Rating: Satisfactory.**

**4.7 Cathodic Protection System**

The most recent cathodic protection (CP) survey data for Tank 7, dated February 2023, was provided by the facility and reviewed as part of this inspection. Tank-to-soil potential readings ranged from −0.92V to −1.05V CSE at the survey test stations around the tank perimeter. These readings are within the acceptable range per NACE SP0169 and API 651 criteria, which specify a minimum polarized potential of −0.85V CSE for adequate cathodic protection of the tank bottom exterior.

**Note:** CP system readings assess the level of cathodic protection provided to the external (soil-side) surface of the tank bottom. CP readings do not assess internal surface conditions of the tank bottom or shell.

**Rating: Satisfactory.**

**[Section 5: API 653 Compliance Checklist]{.underline}**

The following checklist summarizes the compliance status of Tank 7 with respect to applicable API 653 requirements evaluated during this external inspection:

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Item**                **Requirement**                                                                    **Status**
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------
  1                       External visual inspection completed per API 653 § 6.3                             Pass

  2                       Shell condition --- no visible distortion, buckling, or bulging                    Pass

  3                       Shell condition --- no through-wall corrosion or leaks                             Pass

  4                       Foundation --- no excessive settlement or foundation defects                       Pass

  5                       Roof condition --- structurally sound, no ponding                                  Pass

  6                       Appurtenances --- functional, no leaks                                             Pass

  7                       Secondary containment --- adequate, no evidence of release                         Pass

  8                       Cathodic protection --- within acceptable parameters (per most recent CP survey)   Pass

  9                       Previous inspection recommendations addressed                                      Pass

  10                      Internal inspection current per API 653 schedule                                   N/A
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Note to Item 9:** The prior external inspection (June 2021, Report No. CTIS-2021-0608-GF07) had no outstanding action items or unresolved recommendations.

**Note to Item 10:** The next internal inspection for Tank 7 is due approximately 2028--2029 per corrosion rate calculations and remaining thickness evaluations from the most recent internal inspection (March 2019, Report No. CTIS-2019-0314-GF07). An internal inspection was not due at the time of this external inspection and was therefore not performed.

**[Section 6: Recommendations]{.underline}**

Based on the findings of this external inspection, the following recommendations are made:

**Recommendation 1:** Recoat the base ring exterior in the south-southeast quadrant to arrest the minor surface corrosion observed during this inspection. A standard epoxy or polyurethane coating system compatible with the existing coating is recommended. **Priority: Routine --- complete within 90 days.**

**Recommendation 2:** Continue routine external inspection of Tank 7 at 24-month intervals per the facility\'s API 653 inspection program. Next external inspection due: **June 2025.**

**Recommendation 3:** Maintain the cathodic protection system per the current facility schedule. The next CP survey should be conducted per the facility\'s corrosion prevention program.

No recommendation is made for internal inspection, removal of Tank 7 from service, non-destructive examination of weld seams, or any emergency or accelerated corrective action. Based on the findings of this external inspection, Tank 7 is suitable for continued service. No conditions were identified that would require the tank to be removed from service or that would require advancement of the next scheduled internal inspection.

**[Section 7: Certification]{.underline}**

I hereby certify that the inspection documented in this report was performed in accordance with API Standard 653, *Tank Inspection, Repair, Alteration, and Reconstruction*, and that the findings and recommendations stated herein accurately reflect the conditions observed on the date of inspection, June 12, 2023.

**INSPECTOR**

Certification No.: 48172

Fax: (504) 833-4105

Email: inspections@coastaltank.com

**Distribution:** Greenfield Specialty Chemicals, Inc. --- Attention: Ray Fontenot, Maintenance Supervisor

**[Appendix A: Photographic Documentation]{.underline}**

The following photographs were taken during the inspection of Tank 7 on June 12, 2023. Photographs are maintained on file at Coastal Tank Inspection Services, LLC and have been provided to the Client under separate cover.

  ----------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  4                                   Close-up of base ring exterior corrosion, south-southeast quadrant

  6                                   Roof condition --- general view from top of ladder

  8                                   Secondary containment area --- no evidence of release

Photographs 3 and 4 depict the minor surface corrosion on the exterior of the base ring as described in Section 4.2 of this report.

210	**[I. JURISDICTIONAL AND STATUTORY AUTHORITY]{.underline}**
211	
212	The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (\"LDEQ\" or \"the Department\") is an agency of the State of Louisiana charged with the protection of public health and the environment through the regulation of activities that may cause or contribute to pollution. The Department acts pursuant to, and exercises its authority under, the Louisiana Environmental Quality Act, La. R.S. 30:2001 *et seq.*, and specifically La. R.S. 30:2025, which grants the Department the authority to issue compliance orders to persons who are in violation of, or who have caused conditions that violate, the provisions of the Louisiana Environmental Quality Act, rules, regulations, or permits issued thereunder. The Department further acts pursuant to its authority under La. R.S. 30:2050 *et seq.*, which governs the regulation of hazardous waste and hazardous substances within the State of Louisiana, and the Louisiana Administrative Code, Title 33 (Environmental Regulatory Code), Part V (Hazardous Waste and Hazardous Materials) and Part IX (Water Quality).
213	
214	The Secretary of the Department of Environmental Quality, acting through the Office of Environmental Compliance, hereby issues this Compliance Order. This Order is issued under the authority and direction of **Robert J. Melancon, Assistant Secretary, Office of Environmental Compliance**, who has been duly delegated the authority to act on behalf of the Secretary in matters of environmental enforcement and compliance.
215	
216	**[II. RESPONDENT IDENTIFICATION]{.underline}**
217	
218	The Respondent in this matter is **Greenfield Specialty Chemicals, Inc.** (\"Greenfield\" or \"Respondent\"), a Louisiana corporation organized and existing under the laws of the State of Louisiana since 2009, with its principal place of business and subject facility located at **2750 Industrial Canal Road, Belle Chasse, Louisiana 70037**, situated in **Plaquemines Parish**, Louisiana (the \"Subject Facility\"). Greenfield is engaged in the manufacture of specialty chemical intermediates for the petrochemical and agricultural sectors, including amine-based solvents and chemical compounds used in gas treatment, industrial processing, and agrochemical formulation.
219	
220	Greenfield holds Louisiana hazardous materials handling permit number **HM-PQ-2019-0427**, issued by the Department, authorizing Greenfield to store, handle, and process hazardous chemical substances at the Subject Facility. The Subject Facility is a regulated facility under the Louisiana Environmental Quality Act and applicable provisions of the Louisiana Administrative Code. Greenfield is subject to the jurisdiction and regulatory oversight of the Department with respect to all environmental matters arising from its operations at the Subject Facility.
221	
222	**[III. FINDINGS OF FACT]{.underline}**
223	
224	The Department, based upon its investigation, emergency site assessment, review of facility records, and information obtained from Greenfield and other sources, makes the following Findings of Fact:
225	
226	**1.** On **March 14, 2025, at approximately 2:17 a.m. Central Standard Time (CST)**, a catastrophic structural failure occurred at **Tank 7**, a **50,000-gallon carbon steel above-ground storage tank** located within the tank farm area of the Subject Facility. Tank 7 was used for the storage of **methyldiethanolamine (\"MDEA\")**, a liquid amine compound utilized in gas sweetening processes and other industrial applications. The structural failure involved a sudden and complete rupture of the tank shell at or near the base of the tank, resulting in the loss of structural integrity of the containment vessel.
227	
228	**2.** The structural failure of Tank 7 resulted in the rapid, uncontrolled release of **approximately 38,000 gallons of MDEA** onto the ground surface and into the surrounding area of the tank farm at the Subject Facility. The released MDEA spread across the floor of the tank farm\'s secondary containment area, overwhelmed the secondary containment berm in at least two locations, and flowed onto adjacent unpaved surfaces, including the drainage swale running south of the tank farm and the unpaved access road between the tank farm and the main processing building.
229	
230	**3.** The released MDEA contacted an adjacent electrical junction box located approximately forty (40) feet southeast of Tank 7, causing an arc flash and subsequent fire. The fire spread rapidly to **Tank 6**, a carbon steel above-ground storage tank located adjacent to Tank 7, which at the time of the incident contained **approximately 25,000 gallons of monoethanolamine (\"MEA\")**. The fire caused the partial failure of Tank 6, including a breach of the tank shell along the upper third of the vessel, resulting in the additional release of MEA into the environment. The fire also caused significant thermal and structural damage to a pipe rack connecting the tank farm to the main processing building, rendering the pipe rack and associated piping systems inoperable. The fire was suppressed by the Plaquemines Parish Fire Department and Greenfield\'s on-site emergency response team by approximately 5:40 a.m. on March 14, 2025.
231	
232	**4.** MDEA (Chemical Abstracts Service Registry Number 105-59-9) and MEA (Chemical Abstracts Service Registry Number 141-43-5) are **hazardous chemical substances** as defined under the Louisiana Environmental Quality Act and applicable provisions of the Louisiana Administrative Code. Both substances are classified as chemical irritants and contaminants posing risks to human health and the environment upon uncontrolled release. MDEA is a tertiary amine that is harmful upon dermal contact and ingestion and poses documented environmental risks to aquatic organisms and soil biota when released in significant concentrations into soil and water. MEA is a primary amine classified as a **corrosive substance and an acute toxicant** that poses significant risks to human health and the environment upon uncontrolled release, including severe irritation and burns upon dermal and ocular contact, respiratory distress upon inhalation of vapors, and acute toxicity to aquatic life at low concentrations. Both MDEA and MEA are regulated chemicals under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (\"CERCLA\"), 42 U.S.C. § 9601 *et seq.*, and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act (\"EPCRA\"), 42 U.S.C. § 11001 *et seq.*, and both substances are listed on the Toxic Release Inventory (\"TRI\") maintained by the United States Environmental Protection Agency. The Department classifies the combined MDEA and MEA release at the Subject Facility as a **release of hazardous chemical substances** requiring remedial action under Louisiana law.
233	
234	**5.** The Department conducted an emergency site assessment at the Subject Facility on **March 15 through March 17, 2025**. During the emergency assessment, Department personnel collected soil samples from multiple locations within and adjacent to the tank farm area, including the drainage swale and the unpaved access road. Laboratory analysis of soil samples revealed MDEA concentrations of up to **14,200 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg)** and MEA concentrations of up to **8,700 mg/kg**, both significantly exceeding the Department\'s Risk Evaluation/Corrective Action Program (\"RECAP\") screening standards for soil applicable to industrial sites. Groundwater monitoring wells installed during the emergency assessment in the shallow aquifer beneath the Subject Facility revealed MDEA concentrations of **3,400 micrograms per liter (µg/L)** and MEA concentrations of **1,850 µg/L**, both exceeding applicable groundwater screening standards established under the RECAP program.
235	
236	**6.** Based upon the results of the emergency site assessment, the Department has determined that contamination resulting from the March 14, 2025 release extends across **approximately 2.8 acres** of the Subject Facility, encompassing the tank farm, the drainage swale running south of the tank farm, and portions of the unpaved access road between the tank farm and the main processing building. Shallow groundwater contamination has been identified in at least **four (4) monitoring locations** within the Subject Facility boundary. The full lateral and vertical extent of the groundwater contamination plume has not yet been delineated and will require additional investigation.
237	
238	**7.** The Department has determined that the contamination at the Subject Facility poses an **ongoing risk to human health and the environment**, including the potential migration of contaminants through the subsurface to adjacent surface water bodies, including drainage canals and waterways connected to the Intracoastal Waterway system, and to deeper groundwater aquifers that may serve as current or future sources of drinking water. The risk of continued migration is exacerbated by the permeable nature of the shallow soils at the Subject Facility and the proximity of the contamination to the drainage swale, which connects to off-site surface water features.
239	
240	**[IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW / VIOLATIONS]{.underline}**
241	
242	Based upon the foregoing Findings of Fact, the Department reaches the following Conclusions of Law:
243	
244	**1.** Greenfield\'s release of approximately 38,000 gallons of MDEA and additional quantities of MEA from Tank 7 and Tank 6 at the Subject Facility constitutes an unauthorized discharge of hazardous chemical substances into the environment in violation of La. R.S. 30:2025(A), which prohibits the unauthorized discharge, emission, disposal, or release of any pollutant, contaminant, or hazardous substance into the air, water, or onto land within the State of Louisiana. The release of MDEA and MEA onto the ground surface, into the drainage swale, and into the subsurface soil and shallow groundwater at the Subject Facility constitutes a violation of this prohibition.
245	
246	**2.** The contamination of soil and groundwater at the Subject Facility, as documented in the Department\'s emergency site assessment and described in the Findings of Fact herein, constitutes a **Pollution Condition** as that term is understood under Louisiana environmental law --- specifically, the discharge, dispersal, release, or escape of pollutants into or upon land, into the atmosphere, or into any watercourse, body of water, or groundwater. The release of MDEA and MEA, both of which are hazardous chemical substances, irritants, contaminants, and pollutants, resulted in a new pollution condition at the Subject Facility on March 14, 2025. The concentrations of MDEA and MEA detected in soil and groundwater during the Department\'s emergency assessment significantly exceed applicable RECAP screening standards, confirming the existence of a pollution condition requiring remediation. The Department\'s investigation has identified no evidence of any pre-existing contamination by MDEA or MEA at the Subject Facility prior to the March 14, 2025 incident; accordingly, the pollution condition described herein originated from the events of March 14, 2025.
247	
248	**3.** Greenfield failed to immediately and directly report the release to the Department as required by La. R.S. 30:2025(E) and LAC 33:I.3925, which require that any person responsible for a discharge or release of a hazardous substance shall immediately notify the Department by the most rapid means available. The Department acknowledges that Greenfield\'s facility emergency response team notified the Louisiana State Police Emergency Services Unit at approximately 3:05 a.m. on March 14, 2025, and that the Department received notification of the incident through the state emergency response network at approximately 6:30 a.m. on March 14, 2025. While the Department considers the notification to have been substantially compliant with the spirit of the reporting requirement, the failure to directly contact the Department constitutes a technical violation of the direct reporting obligation under La. R.S. 30:2025(E) and LAC 33:I.3925.
249	
250	**[V. ORDER / REQUIRED ACTIONS]{.underline}**
251	
252	Based upon the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, the Department hereby ORDERS as follows:
253	
254	**1. Immediate Actions.** Greenfield was directed to cease all operations in the affected tank farm area immediately upon the release and to implement emergency containment measures to prevent further migration of released MDEA and MEA. The Department acknowledges that Greenfield implemented emergency containment measures, including the deployment of earthen berms, absorbent materials, and temporary barriers, within hours of the March 14, 2025 incident. Greenfield shall maintain all emergency containment measures in place until such time as the Department authorizes their removal or modification.
255	
256	**2. Site Access Restrictions During Initial Assessment and Remediation Planning.** The Department hereby orders that **no industrial operations, manufacturing activities, construction, repair, reconstruction, demolition, or any other physical work activities** shall be conducted within the **Affected Area** until the Department has completed its initial environmental assessment and has approved a Remedial Action Plan as described in Paragraph 4 of this Section. The **Affected Area** is defined as the tank farm (including all tanks, secondary containment structures, and associated equipment within the tank farm perimeter), the drainage swale running south of the tank farm, the pipe rack corridor connecting the tank farm to the main processing building, and the unpaved access road between the tank farm and the main processing building. Access to the Affected Area shall be limited exclusively to:
257	
258	> \(a\) LDEQ personnel and authorized representatives of the Department;
259	>
260	> \(b\) Greenfield\'s designated environmental consultant and its employees or subcontractors performing environmental investigation or monitoring activities approved by the Department;
261	>
262	> \(c\) Emergency safety personnel responding to any immediate threat to human health or safety; and
263	>
264	> \(d\) Such other persons as the Department may specifically authorize in writing.
265	
266	**No person shall conduct, authorize, or permit any industrial operations, equipment repair, tank replacement, construction, or reconstruction activities within the Affected Area during the pendency of this restriction.** This restriction shall remain in effect until the Department provides written notice to Greenfield of its approval of the Remedial Action Plan or until the Department otherwise modifies or lifts this restriction by written notice. Greenfield shall ensure that the Affected Area is physically secured against unauthorized entry by means of fencing, barricades, signage, or other appropriate measures.
267	
268	**3. Remedial Investigation.** Within **thirty (30) days** of the date of this Order (i.e., by **May 3, 2025**), Greenfield shall submit to the Department a comprehensive Remedial Investigation Work Plan, prepared by a qualified environmental professional licensed in the State of Louisiana, detailing the scope and methodology of additional soil and groundwater sampling to be conducted at the Subject Facility, the proposed approach for delineation of the lateral and vertical extent of the MDEA and MEA contamination plume, the risk assessment methodology to be employed, and a proposed schedule for completion of the remedial investigation. The Remedial Investigation Work Plan shall comply with the requirements of the Department\'s RECAP program and all applicable provisions of LAC 33:Part I, Chapter 13.
269	
270	**4. Remedial Action Plan.** Within **ninety (90) days** of the date of this Order (i.e., by **July 2, 2025**), Greenfield shall submit to the Department a Remedial Action Plan (\"RAP\") for the remediation and cleanup of all contaminated soil and groundwater at the Subject Facility. The RAP shall propose remediation methods and performance standards sufficient to achieve cleanup of all contaminated media to levels meeting the Department\'s RECAP screening standards applicable to industrial sites, or such other risk-based standards as the Department may approve. The RAP shall include a detailed implementation schedule, cost estimates, and a description of all engineering controls and institutional controls proposed for the Subject Facility.
271	
272	**5. Completion of Remediation.** Greenfield shall complete all remediation activities described in the approved RAP within **eighteen (18) months** of the date of this Order (i.e., by **October 3, 2026**). Upon completion of remediation, Greenfield shall submit to the Department a Remediation Completion Report, including analytical results from confirmatory sampling, demonstrating that the remediation has achieved the cleanup standards specified in the approved RAP. The Department may grant reasonable extensions of the remediation completion deadline upon a showing of good cause by Greenfield, provided that any request for extension is submitted in writing to the Department at least thirty (30) days prior to the applicable deadline.
273	
274	**6. Reporting Requirements.** Greenfield shall submit quarterly progress reports to the Department during the remediation period, describing the status of all investigation and remediation activities, including a summary of analytical data collected during the reporting period, a description of any deviations from the approved RAP, and a projection of remaining work. The first quarterly progress report shall be due on **July 3, 2025**, and subsequent reports shall be due on the first business day of each calendar quarter thereafter until the Department issues written confirmation that all remediation obligations under this Order have been satisfied.
275	
276	**7. Financial Responsibility.** Greenfield shall demonstrate financial responsibility for the estimated cost of remediation at the Subject Facility. The Department notes that preliminary cost estimates provided by Greenfield\'s environmental consultant, submitted to the Department on March 28, 2025, indicate total estimated remediation costs of **approximately Four Million Two Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$4,200,000)**. Within **forty-five (45) days** of the date of this Order, Greenfield shall provide to the Department evidence of adequate financial assurance for the full estimated cost of remediation, which may take the form of environmental insurance coverage, a surety bond, an irrevocable letter of credit, a corporate guarantee meeting the Department\'s financial assurance requirements, or such other form of financial assurance as the Department may approve.
277	
278	**[VI. PENALTIES AND ENFORCEMENT]{.underline}**
279	
280	The Department reserves the right to assess civil penalties of up to **Thirty-Two Thousand Five Hundred Dollars (\$32,500) per day of violation** pursuant to La. R.S. 30:2025(H) for any failure by Greenfield to comply with the terms, conditions, and deadlines set forth in this Order. Each day of continued non-compliance shall constitute a separate violation for purposes of penalty assessment.
281	
282	Failure to comply with the deadlines and requirements set forth herein may result in additional enforcement action by the Department, including but not limited to the issuance of additional compliance orders, the assessment of stipulated penalties, and referral of this matter to the Louisiana Attorney General for judicial enforcement in the courts of the State of Louisiana.
283	
284	The issuance of this Compliance Order does not preclude the Department from taking additional or separate enforcement action, or from assessing civil penalties, for the underlying violations described herein. The Department expressly reserves all enforcement rights and remedies available under the Louisiana Environmental Quality Act and applicable regulations.
285	
286	**[VII. RIGHT TO REQUEST A HEARING]{.underline}**
287	
288	Greenfield has the right to request an adjudicatory hearing before the Department pursuant to La. R.S. 30:2050.21 and the Louisiana Administrative Procedure Act, La. R.S. 49:950 *et seq.* Any request for a hearing must be made in writing and filed with the Department within **thirty (30) days** of the Respondent\'s receipt of this Order. Fifth Street, Baton Rouge, Louisiana 70802, with a copy to the Office of Environmental Compliance. If no timely request for a hearing is filed, this Order shall become final and binding upon the Respondent without further notice or proceedings.

    d.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    return t

    H(d, "A. The Loss", 2)
    P(d, "At approximately 2:17 a.m. CST on March 14, 2025, Tank 7 — a 50,000-gallon carbon steel above-ground storage tank built in 2011 to API 650 and holding approximately 38,000 gallons of methyldiethanolamine (“MDEA”) — failed at the circumferential weld joining the lowest shell course to the annular (base) ring. The fracture propagated roughly 270 degrees around the circumference (Vector § 4.2). Vector found the failure “abrupt and occurred without prior warning,” with “no alarms,” “no visible precursors such as weeping, seepage, or bulging,” and “no gradual loss of tank contents,” and on-site personnel reported “a single loud percussive event” (Vector § 4.1; Concl. 4). LDEQ likewise found “a sudden and complete rupture of the tank shell” (LDEQ Order ¶ III.1).", align="j")
    P(d, "The released MDEA flowed across the secondary containment area and contacted energized Junction Box JB-14, causing an arc flash that ignited MDEA vapors and liquid. The fire engulfed Tank 6 (approximately 25,000 gallons of monoethanolamine, “MEA”), the pipe rack to the main processing building, approximately 1,200 linear feet of electrical conduit and cabling, and the north wall and roof of the processing building (Vector §§ 4.1, 5). Vector concluded that “the majority of the physical damage to structures and equipment other than Tank 7 itself was caused by the fire and thermal exposure,” and that direct damage from MDEA contact “was limited to the tank farm secondary containment berm area, the soil beneath and surrounding Tank 7, and Junction Box JB-14 itself” (Vector § 5, “Damage Causation”; Concl. 9). Firewater runoff carried MDEA-contaminated water beyond the berm through a drain valve compromised during the event (Vector § 4.1).", align="j")
    H(d, "B. Cause: Internal Corrosion Undetectable by External Inspection", 2)
    P(d, "Vector attributes the failure to internal (product-side) corrosion at the shell-to-annular-ring weld and heat-affected zone, with morphology consistent with microbiologically influenced corrosion (“MIC”) and/or amine stress corrosion cracking (“SCC”), reducing wall thickness from 0.375 in. to as little as 0.087 in. (a 77% loss) in a localized area, while remote readings were 0.310–0.355 in. (Vector § 4.2; Concls. 1–3). Vector estimates — expressly “preliminary,” pending metallurgical analysis expected in 4–6 weeks — that the corrosion developed over approximately 3–5 years (Vector §§ 1, 4.2, 7). Vector found the corrosion “was not visible or detectable through routine external inspection methods” (Concl. 5).", align="j")
    P(d, "Critically, Vector determined that the “minor surface corrosion” noted in the June 2023 CTIS external inspection “is a separate and distinct condition” from the internal weld-seam corrosion, differing “in their location, their corrosion mechanism, and their severity,” and that “they are not related as a matter of engineering analysis” (Vector § 4.3; Concl. 6). Vector also found Greenfield’s inspection program “structured in accordance with API 653,” that external inspections were at proper intervals, that the August 3, 2023 recoat was “appropriate, timely, and consistent with the recommendation,” and that Vector “did not identify any specific deficiency in Greenfield’s inspection or maintenance practices” (Vector § 4.4; Concls. 7–8). Notably, the Vector report contains no finding regarding “inadequate cathodic protection,” which the Letter attributes to it.", align="j")
    H(d, "C. Inspection and Maintenance History", 2)
    P(d, "CTIS performed an internal API 653 inspection in March 2019 (Report CTIS-2019-0314-GF07), from which the next internal inspection was calculated to fall due in approximately 2028–2029 (CTIS 2023 §§ 1, 5 n. 10; CMMS § 1 lists March 2029). The June 12, 2023 external inspection was “external visual inspection only,” rated the shell “Satisfactory,” found “minor surface corrosion” on the base ring exterior (about 3 feet of arc in the south-southeast quadrant) with “[n]o weeping, seepage, product staining, measurable wall loss, or evidence of through-wall corrosion,” recommended recoating within 90 days and monitoring at the next external inspection (June 2025), and expressly made “[n]o recommendation … for internal inspection” or for advancing the next internal inspection (CTIS 2023 §§ 1, 4.2, 6). Greenfield opened WO-2023-0471 on June 30, 2023 (approved by Plant Manager K. Tran) and completed a two-coat epoxy recoat on August 3, 2023 — well inside the 90-day window that ran to September 10, 2023 (CMMS Entries 2.6–2.7). Monthly operator rounds from January 2022 to February 2025 found no anomalies; the last, on February 15, 2025, found the base-ring coating intact (CMMS Entries 2.9, 2.11). Annual cathodic protection (“CP”) surveys in 2022, 2023, and 2024 were within NACE SP0169 criteria, though the October 2024 southeast-quadrant reading (−0.85 V CSE) was at the threshold and flagged for monitoring (CMMS Entries 2.4, 2.8, 2.10). CTIS notes that CP protects only the external soil-side surface of the tank bottom and does not address internal surfaces (CTIS 2023 § 4.7).", align="j")
    H(d, "D. Notice, Claims, and Regulatory Response", 2)
    P(d, "Greenfield’s General Counsel instructed the broker at 8:45 a.m. on March 14, 2025 to give notice under both policies; Tidewater Risk Advisors gave written notice to claims@pinnacleassurance.com at 11:00 a.m. the same day, identifying both policies, the date, time, location, description of the incident, and preliminary damage, environmental, and BI information. Pinnacle retained Crossfield and Vector on March 20; Vector inspected the site March 22–24 and April 8–9, 2025, collected specimens under chain-of-custody protocols, took 143 photographs, and interviewed personnel (Vector §§ 1, 3).", align="j")
    P(d, "LDEQ conducted an emergency assessment March 15–17, 2025 and on April 3, 2025 issued Compliance Order CO-2025-0341, finding MDEA and MEA to be “hazardous chemical substances,” documenting soil and groundwater contamination exceeding RECAP standards across approximately 2.8 acres, finding “no evidence of any pre-existing contamination by MDEA or MEA,” prohibiting all industrial operations, repair, and reconstruction in the “Affected Area” (tank farm, drainage swale, pipe rack corridor, and access road) pending approval of a Remedial Action Plan, and requiring a Remedial Investigation Work Plan (by May 3, 2025), a RAP (by July 2, 2025), financial assurance (within 45 days), and completion of remediation by October 3, 2026 (LDEQ Order ¶¶ III.4–III.6, IV.2, V.2–V.7). Greenfield submitted a sworn CP proof of loss on April 10, 2025 ($25.5 million) and a PLL claim on April 18, 2025 ($4.2 million). The facility was fully shut down through May 1, 2025 and resumed operations at 40% capacity on May 2, 2025. Pinnacle issued its “final” denial on May 9, 2025 — eleven days after receiving Vector’s preliminary report and before the metallurgical results.", align="j")

    H(d, "A. CP Policy", 2)
    P(d, "The CP Policy is written on an “all risks” basis: “all risks of direct physical loss of or damage to Covered Property are covered unless specifically excluded,” and “[t]he burden of proving that a loss falls within the scope of an exclusion or limitation shall rest with the Insurer” (§ I). Each tank, pipe rack, electrical system, building, and item of equipment “constitutes a separate item of Covered Property,” and coverage “applies independently to each” (§ II.C). Key terms: Property Damage limit $50,000,000 per Occurrence; deductible $250,000 per Occurrence (PD only); BI limit $15,000,000 per Occurrence (separate); 72-hour BI waiting period in lieu of deductible (§§ III.A–B, VI.D–E). The Ensuing Loss Provision (final paragraph of § IV) provides that “[n]otwithstanding the foregoing exclusions,” if an excluded cause “results in a Covered Cause of Loss, this Policy covers the loss or damage caused by that Covered Cause of Loss,” expressly including “fire, explosion,” “regardless of the sequence of events or the number of intervening causes,” provided the covered cause is “a natural and reasonably foreseeable consequence of the excluded cause of loss.” BI coverage follows covered PD “including by operation of the Ensuing Loss Provision” (§§ VI.A, VI.G).", align="j")
    H(d, "B. PLL Policy", 2)
    P(d, "The PLL Policy is claims-made-and-reported. Limits are $10,000,000 per Claim and aggregate, eroded by defense costs, subject to a $150,000 SIR (Declarations; § VI).", align="j")

    P(d, "**Assumptions and limitations.** (1) We have only policy excerpts; both excerpts state that the complete policy controls, and several potentially significant endorsements (CP: Louisiana Amendatory Endorsement PNN-CP-END-005, Equipment Breakdown Enhancement PNN-CP-END-006, Ordinance or Law PNN-CP-END-007, Debris Removal PNN-CP-END-008, Extra Expense PNN-CP-END-009; PLL: omitted Sections I.D–I.F, II.C–II.F, II.H–II.L, II.Q–II.T, IV.C–IV.H, V.B, V.D–V.E, V.I–V.K, VII.E–VII.J) have not been reviewed. (2) The file reflects events through May 2025; we have no information about subsequent developments (Vector’s final report and metallurgical results, any reconsideration request, LDEQ progress, actual BI results). (3) Louisiana law is assumed to govern both policies (the PLL Policy so provides at § VII.B; the CP Policy carries a Louisiana Amendatory Endorsement and insures Louisiana risks). Legal authorities cited below are identified from general knowledge and must be cite-checked and confirmed against current statutory text before use in any external communication.", align="j")

    H(d, "III. Factual Background", 1)
    H(d, "A. The Loss", 2)
    P(d, "At approximately 2:17 a.m. CST on March 14, 2025, Tank 7 — a 50,000-gallon carbon steel above-ground storage tank built in 2011 to API 650 and holding approximately 38,000 gallons of methyldiethanolamine (“MDEA”) — failed at the circumferential weld joining the lowest shell course to the annular (base) ring. The fracture propagated roughly 270 degrees around the circumference (Vector § 4.2). Vector found the failure “abrupt and occurred without prior warning,” with “no alarms,” “no visible precursors such as weeping, seepage, or bulging,” and “no gradual loss of tank contents,” and on-site personnel reported “a single loud percussive event” (Vector § 4.1; Concl. 4). LDEQ likewise found “a sudden and complete rupture of the tank shell” (LDEQ Order ¶ III.1).", align="j")
    P(d, "The released MDEA flowed across the secondary containment area and contacted energized Junction Box JB-14, causing an arc flash that ignited MDEA vapors and liquid. The fire engulfed Tank 6 (approximately 25,000 gallons of monoethanolamine, “MEA”), the pipe rack to the main processing building, approximately 1,200 linear feet of electrical conduit and cabling, and the north wall and roof of the processing building (Vector §§ 4.1, 5). Vector concluded that “the majority of the physical damage to structures and equipment other than Tank 7 itself was caused by the fire and thermal exposure,” and that direct damage from MDEA contact “was limited to the tank farm secondary containment berm area, the soil beneath and surrounding Tank 7, and Junction Box JB-14 itself” (Vector § 5, “Damage Causation”; Concl. 9). Firewater runoff carried MDEA-contaminated water beyond the berm through a drain valve compromised during the event (Vector § 4.1).", align="j")
    H(d, "B. Cause: Internal Corrosion Undetectable by External Inspection", 2)
    P(d, "Vector attributes the failure to internal (product-side) corrosion at the shell-to-annular-ring weld and heat-affected zone, with morphology consistent with microbiologically influenced corrosion (“MIC”) and/or amine stress corrosion cracking (“SCC”), reducing wall thickness from 0.375 in. to as little as 0.087 in. (a 77% loss) in a localized area, while remote readings were 0.310–0.355 in. (Vector § 4.2; Concls. 1–3). Vector estimates — expressly “preliminary,” pending metallurgical analysis expected in 4–6 weeks — that the corrosion developed over approximately 3–5 years (Vector §§ 1, 4.2, 7). Vector found the corrosion “was not visible or detectable through routine external inspection methods” (Concl. 5).", align="j")
    P(d, "Critically, Vector determined that the “minor surface corrosion” noted in the June 2023 CTIS external inspection “is a separate and distinct condition” from the internal weld-seam corrosion, differing “in their location, their corrosion mechanism, and their severity,” and that “they are not related as a matter of engineering analysis” (Vector § 4.3; Concl. 6). Vector also found Greenfield’s inspection program “structured in accordance with API 653,” that external inspections were at proper intervals, that the August 3, 2023 recoat was “appropriate, timely, and consistent with the recommendation,” and that Vector “did not identify any specific deficiency in Greenfield’s inspection or maintenance practices” (Vector § 4.4; Concls. 7–8). Notably, the Vector report contains no finding regarding “inadequate cathodic protection,” which the Letter attributes to it.", align="j")
    H(d, "C. Inspection and Maintenance History", 2)
    P(d, "CTIS performed an internal API 653 inspection in March 2019 (Report CTIS-2019-0314-GF07), from which the next internal inspection was calculated to fall due in approximately 2028–2029 (CTIS 2023 §§ 1, 5 n. 10; CMMS § 1 lists March 2029). The June 12, 2023 external inspection was “external visual inspection only,” rated the shell “Satisfactory,” found “minor surface corrosion” on the base ring exterior (about 3 feet of arc in the south-southeast quadrant) with “[n]o weeping, seepage, product staining, measurable wall loss, or evidence of through-wall corrosion,” recommended recoating within 90 days and monitoring at the next external inspection (June 2025), and expressly made “[n]o recommendation … for internal inspection” or for advancing the next internal inspection (CTIS 2023 §§ 1, 4.2, 6). Greenfield opened WO-2023-0471 on June 30, 2023 (approved by Plant Manager K. Tran) and completed a two-coat epoxy recoat on August 3, 2023 — well inside the 90-day window that ran to September 10, 2023 (CMMS Entries 2.6–2.7). Monthly operator rounds from January 2022 to February 2025 found no anomalies; the last, on February 15, 2025, found the base-ring coating intact (CMMS Entries 2.9, 2.11). Annual cathodic protection (“CP”) surveys in 2022, 2023, and 2024 were within NACE SP0169 criteria, though the October 2024 southeast-quadrant reading (−0.85 V CSE) was at the threshold and flagged for monitoring (CMMS Entries 2.4, 2.8, 2.10). CTIS notes that CP protects only the external soil-side surface of the tank bottom and does not address internal surfaces (CTIS 2023 § 4.7).", align="j")
    H(d, "D. Notice, Claims, and Regulatory Response", 2)
    P(d, "Greenfield’s General Counsel instructed the broker at 8:45 a.m. on March 14, 2025 to give notice under both policies; Tidewater Risk Advisors gave written notice to claims@pinnacleassurance.com at 11:00 a.m. the same day, identifying both policies, the date, time, location, description of the incident, and preliminary damage, environmental, and BI information. On March 15, 2025, Pinnacle acknowledged “receipt of the notice of loss,” opened Claim File CLM-2025-07744, “recorded [it] against both” policies, assigned Ms. Kwan, and requested evidence preservation. Pinnacle retained Crossfield and Vector on March 20; Vector inspected the site March 22–24 and April 8–9, 2025, collected specimens under chain-of-custody protocols, took 143 photographs, and interviewed personnel (Vector §§ 1, 3).", align="j")
    P(d, "LDEQ conducted an emergency assessment March 15–17, 2025 and on April 3, 2025 issued Compliance Order CO-2025-0341, finding MDEA and MEA to be “hazardous chemical substances,” documenting soil and groundwater contamination exceeding RECAP standards across approximately 2.8 acres, finding “no evidence of any pre-existing contamination by MDEA or MEA,” prohibiting all industrial operations, repair, and reconstruction in the “Affected Area” (tank farm, drainage swale, pipe rack corridor, and access road) pending approval of a Remedial Action Plan, and requiring a Remedial Investigation Work Plan (by May 3, 2025), a RAP (by July 2, 2025), financial assurance (within 45 days), and completion of remediation by October 3, 2026 (LDEQ Order ¶¶ III.4–III.6, IV.2, V.2–V.7). Greenfield submitted a sworn CP proof of loss on April 10, 2025 ($25.5 million) and a PLL claim on April 18, 2025 ($4.2 million). The facility was fully shut down through May 1, 2025 and resumed operations at 40% capacity on May 2, 2025. Pinnacle issued its “final” denial on May 9, 2025 — eleven days after receiving Vector’s preliminary report and before the metallurgical results.", align="j")
    H(d, "E. Chronology", 2)
    T(d, ["Date", "Event", "Source"], [
        ["2011", "Tank 7 constructed (API 650; carbon steel)", "CTIS 2023 § 2"],
        ["Mar. 2019", "CTIS internal inspection; next internal calculated for ~2028–2029 (CMMS: Mar. 2029)", "CTIS 2023 §§ 1, 5; CMMS § 1"],
        ["June/July 2021", "External inspection; no action items (CTIS: June 2021; CMMS: July 14, 2021)", "CTIS 2023 § 2; CMMS 2.3"],
        ["Jan. 2022–Feb. 2025", "Monthly operator rounds; no anomalies", "CMMS 2.2, 2.9, 2.11"],
        ["June 12, 2023", "CTIS external inspection; minor exterior base-ring surface corrosion; recoat within 90 days", "CTIS 2023 §§ 4.2, 6"],
        ["Aug. 3, 2023", "Base-ring exterior recoat completed (WO-2023-0471)", "CMMS 2.7; Vector § 4.3"],
        ["Oct. 11, 2024", "CP survey within criteria; SE quadrant at threshold, monitor", "CMMS 2.10"],

        ["Mar. 14, 2025, 11:00 a.m.", "Broker’s written notice of loss to Pinnacle under both policies", "Email chain"],
        ["Mar. 15, 2025", "Pinnacle acknowledges notice; opens CLM-2025-07744 under both policies", "Email chain"],
        ["Mar. 20–24, 2025", "Pinnacle retains Crossfield/Vector; Vector site inspection and specimen collection", "Vector §§ 1, 3"],
        ["Apr. 3, 2025", "LDEQ Compliance Order (a “Claim” under PLL § II.A(3))", "LDEQ Order"],
        ["Apr. 10, 2025", "Sworn proof of loss (CP) — day 27 of 90", "Letter § III"],
        ["Apr. 18, 2025", "PLL claim submitted", "Letter § III"],
        ["Apr. 28, 2025", "Vector preliminary report; metallurgy pending", "Vector §§ 1, 7"],
        ["May 2, 2025", "Partial operations resume at 40%", "BI workbook; Letter § II"],
        ["May 9, 2025", "Pinnacle denial (29 days after proof of loss)", "Letter"],
        ["~May 18, 2025", "LDEQ financial-assurance deadline (45 days)", "LDEQ ¶ V.7"],
        ["Aug. 15, 2025", "Projected full restoration (BI period end)", "BI Summary"],
        ["Oct. 3, 2026", "LDEQ remediation completion deadline (passed — status unknown)", "LDEQ ¶ V.5"],
        ["Mar. 14, 2027 (Sun.)", "Two-year CP suit-limitation date (§ V.E)", "CP Policy § V.E"],
    ], [1.3, 3.9, 1.3], size=9)

    H(d, "IV. Policy Framework and Interpretive Principles", 1)
    H(d, "A. CP Policy", 2)
    P(d, "The CP Policy is written on an “all risks” basis: “all risks of direct physical loss of or damage to Covered Property are covered unless specifically excluded,” and “[t]he burden of proving that a loss falls within the scope of an exclusion or limitation shall rest with the Insurer” (§ I). Each tank, pipe rack, electrical system, building, and item of equipment “constitutes a separate item of Covered Property,” and coverage “applies independently to each” (§ II.C). Key terms: Property Damage limit $50,000,000 per Occurrence; deductible $250,000 per Occurrence (PD only); BI limit $15,000,000 per Occurrence (separate); 72-hour BI waiting period in lieu of deductible (§§ III.A–B, VI.D–E). The Ensuing Loss Provision (final paragraph of § IV) provides that “[n]otwithstanding the foregoing exclusions,” if an excluded cause “results in a Covered Cause of Loss, this Policy covers the loss or damage caused by that Covered Cause of Loss,” expressly including “fire, explosion,” “regardless of the sequence of events or the number of intervening causes,” provided the covered cause is “a natural and reasonably foreseeable consequence of the excluded cause of loss.” BI coverage follows covered PD “including by operation of the Ensuing Loss Provision” (§§ VI.A, VI.G).", align="j")
    H(d, "B. PLL Policy", 2)
    P(d, "The PLL Policy is claims-made-and-reported. Pinnacle must pay Remediation Costs and Claim Expenses the Insured becomes legally obligated to pay as a result of a Claim first made and reported during the Policy Period arising from a Pollution Condition at a Covered Location that commenced on or after the January 1, 2017 Retroactive Date (§ I.A). A “Claim” includes a governmental “compliance order” (§ II.A(3)). Pinnacle has “the right and duty to defend” any Claim “even if any of the allegations … are groundless” (§ I.B). Limits are $10,000,000 per Claim and aggregate, eroded by defense costs, subject to a $150,000 SIR (Declarations; § VI).", align="j")
    H(d, "C. Interpretive Principles (Louisiana)", 2)
    B(d, [
        "Insurance policies are construed under the Civil Code’s general rules of contract interpretation (La. C.C. arts. 2045–2057). Words are given their generally prevailing meaning; each provision is interpreted in light of the others so that each is given meaning (art. 2050); and doubtful provisions are construed against the party who furnished the text — here Pinnacle (art. 2056).",
        "The insurer bears the burden of proving an exclusion applies, and exclusions are strictly construed against the insurer. The CP Policy contractually allocates this burden to Pinnacle (§ I). The insured bears the burden on exceptions to exclusions where the policy so provides (CP § IV.J places the Sudden and Accidental burden on Greenfield).",
        "The Louisiana Supreme Court has held that a pollution exclusion is to be applied in light of its purpose of excluding coverage for environmental pollution, considering whether the insured is a “polluter,” whether the substance is a “pollutant,” and whether there was a “discharge, dispersal, seepage, migration, release or escape.” [[Doerr v. Mobil Oil Corp.]], 2000-0947 (La. 12/19/00), 774 So. 2d 119. [Cite-check required.]",

from lib import *

def part2(d):
    H(d, "V. Analysis — CP Policy Denial Grounds", 1)

    H(d, "A. Pollution Exclusion, § IV.J (Letter § IV.A)", 2)
    P(d, "**Pinnacle’s position.** The release of MDEA “initiated the chain of events that caused all of the claimed property damage”; “[b]ut for the discharge of pollutants, no loss would have occurred”; therefore the entire $18.7 million PD claim (and, derivatively, BI) is excluded.", align="j")
    P(d, "**1. The “but-for” theory is foreclosed by the Ensuing Loss Provision, which the Letter never mentions.** The Ensuing Loss Provision applies “[n]otwithstanding the foregoing exclusions set forth in this Section IV,” expressly including § IV.J, and provides that where an excluded cause “results in a fire, explosion, or other Covered Cause of Loss, the direct physical loss or damage caused by such fire, explosion, or other Covered Cause of Loss is covered … regardless of the sequence of events or the number of intervening causes.” Its stated purpose is “to ensure that the Named Insured is not deprived of coverage for otherwise-covered perils merely because such perils were set in motion by an excluded cause of loss.” That is exactly the scenario here. Fire is not excluded anywhere in the excerpts; indeed, §§ IV.F and IV.H confirm that ensuing fire is a covered peril. Pinnacle’s own engineer found that fire was “the principal cause of damage to Tank 6, the pipe rack, the electrical conduit systems, and the processing building” (Vector § 5). The Letter’s statement that the Pollution Exclusion “encompasses not only the direct consequences of the chemical release but also all subsequent damage that flows from” it is irreconcilable with the policy text.", align="j")
    P(d, "**2. Anticipated counter-arguments.** Pinnacle may invoke (a) the § IV preamble (“excluded regardless of any other cause or event that contributes concurrently or in any sequence”) and (b) the Ensuing Loss proviso that the covered cause be “a natural and reasonably foreseeable consequence” of the excluded cause. As to (a), the Ensuing Loss Provision is specific, later in the text, and expressly operates “[n]otwithstanding the foregoing exclusions” and “regardless of the sequence of events”; reading the preamble to swallow it would render the Ensuing Loss Provision meaningless (La. C.C. art. 2050), and any conflict is an ambiguity construed for coverage (art. 2056). As to (b), Pinnacle is poorly positioned to argue the fire was unforeseeable: its Letter characterizes the entire sequence as causally linked and the failure as “inevitable and foreseeable,” and the release of a combustible amine near an energized junction box igniting is the paradigm of a natural consequence.", align="j")
    P(d, "**3. Pinnacle’s inconsistent “pollutant” positions.** In § IV.A the Letter calls MDEA “a chemical pollutant” and MEA “also a chemical pollutant”; in § V.C it declares that MDEA and MEA “are routine process chemicals, not toxic or hazardous substances” and therefore not Pollutants. The CP definition (§ II.K) is broader than the PLL definition (it applies “without regard to the quantity, concentration, or toxicity”), so Greenfield need not dispute that MDEA/MEA are CP “Pollutants.” But the contradiction is powerful evidence that Pinnacle was assembling grounds for denial rather than adjusting the claim, and it supports the extra-contractual claims discussed in Part VIII. (The Letter also paraphrases § II.K inaccurately, inserting “including chemicals and chemical compounds used in industrial processes,” language that does not appear in the definition.)", align="j")
    P(d, "**4. Louisiana law.** Under [[Doerr]], the pollution exclusion is construed in light of its purpose of addressing environmental pollution. Greenfield is a chemical manufacturer and the release did cause environmental contamination, so we would not rely principally on [[Doerr]] for the release itself; but it reinforces that fire damage to Greenfield’s own buildings and equipment is not the “pollution” harm the exclusion targets.", align="j")
    P(d, "**5. What remains potentially excluded.** If the Sudden and Accidental exception were held inapplicable (Part V.B), § IV.J could reach (i) damage caused by direct contact with released MDEA — per Vector, the containment berm area, the soil (likely not Covered Property in any event), and JB-14 — and (ii) cleanup/response costs under § IV.J(2), which belong under the PLL Policy. The Acadian estimate should be segregated so that these items are identified and do not taint the balance of the claim.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Assessment:** Weak as a basis for denying the PD claim; at most a narrow carve-out.", align="j")

    H(d, "B. Sudden and Accidental Exception, § II.L (Letter § IV.B)", 2)
    P(d, "**The Letter misquotes the definition.** It quotes § II.L as “an event that begins abruptly and is not the result of gradual deterioration, wear, or a pre-existing condition known to the insured.” The actual definition requires that the event “begin[ ] abruptly **and without advance warning**,” and then adds two clarifying sentences the Letter omits entirely:", align="j")
    Q(d, "“The term ‘event’ as used in this definition refers to the occurrence giving rise to the loss or damage, not to the underlying or contributing cause of such occurrence. The term ‘known to the Insured’ means actually known to the Named Insured’s management responsible for maintenance and operation of the Covered Property at the relevant Covered Location, and does not include constructive knowledge or information that should have been known through the exercise of reasonable diligence.” (CP § II.L.)")
    P(d, "**Prong 1 — abrupt and without advance warning.** Satisfied by Pinnacle’s own expert: the failure “was abrupt and occurred without prior warning,” with no alarms, no weeping, seepage or bulging, and “a single loud percussive event” (Vector § 4.1; Concl. 4); “[t]he failure event itself — the through-wall fracture and structural rupture — was abrupt, sudden, and instantaneous” (Vector § 4.2). LDEQ independently found a “sudden and complete rupture” (LDEQ ¶ III.1). The Letter’s concession that “the physical manifestation of the tank failure occurred rapidly” confirms the point.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Prong 2 — “pre-existing condition known to the Insured.”** The Letter’s argument fails on the policy’s own definition. Only **actual** knowledge by responsible management counts; constructive knowledge and what “should have been known through the exercise of reasonable diligence” are expressly excluded. The only condition Greenfield knew of was the external surface corrosion noted in June 2023 — which Vector found to be “a separate and distinct condition” that is “not related as a matter of engineering analysis” to the internal weld-seam corrosion that caused the failure (Vector § 4.3; Concl. 6), and which Greenfield remediated by August 3, 2023. The internal corrosion was undetectable by external methods and no one knew of it. The Letter’s premise that Greenfield “did not take adequate steps to investigate” is precisely the “should have known” theory the definition forbids.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Prong 2 — “result of gradual deterioration.”** This is Pinnacle’s best argument and Greenfield’s principal risk under the CP Policy. Vector does say the corrosion developed over approximately 3–5 years. Greenfield has three substantial responses:", align="j")
    N(d, [
        "**The “event” clarification.** The definition instructs that “event” means “the occurrence giving rise to the loss or damage, not … the underlying or contributing cause of such occurrence.” The event is the rupture and release, which was instantaneous. The corrosion is the “underlying … cause” the definition directs the reader to disregard. Reading prong 2 to look through the event to its underlying cause would nullify the clarifying sentence (La. C.C. art. 2050). On this reading, “not the result of gradual deterioration” addresses releases that are themselves gradual — seepage, slow leaks, weeping — which is consistent with the exclusion’s own contrast between releases that are “sudden or gradual.”",
        "**Series qualifier.** “[K]nown to the Insured” can reasonably be read to modify each item in the series “gradual deterioration, wear, or a pre-existing condition.” Under that reading, unknown latent deterioration does not defeat the exception. At a minimum this is a reasonable alternative construction, and ambiguity is resolved against the drafter (La. C.C. art. 2056).",
        "**Prematurity.** The 3–5 year estimate is preliminary and subject to metallurgical analysis (Vector §§ 4.2, 7). Pinnacle denied before the evidence it relied upon was final.",
    ])
    P(d, "**Consequence.** Even if Pinnacle prevailed on this prong, the exception matters only for damage caused directly by the released MDEA. Fire damage is restored by the Ensuing Loss Provision regardless of whether the Sudden and Accidental exception applies. Because Greenfield bears the burden on the exception (§ IV.J), the Vector report and on-site witness testimony should be preserved and developed.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Assessment:** Pinnacle’s known-condition argument is without basis; the gradual-deterioration argument presents moderate risk confined to direct-contact damage.", align="j")

    H(d, "C. Wear and Tear / Corrosion Exclusion, § IV.D (Letter § IV.C)", 2)
    P(d, "**The Letter does not quote the exclusion as written.** It presents § IV.D as a single sentence (“This Policy does not insure against loss or damage caused by or resulting from wear and tear, rust, corrosion …”) and then argues that the “caused by or resulting from” language “extends the exclusion to all consequential losses … not merely to the corroded component itself.” The actual § IV.D contains an operative limitation the Letter omits:", align="j")
    Q(d, "“This exclusion applies to the Covered Property that has experienced the wear and tear, rust, corrosion, deterioration, hidden defect, latent defect, or self-destructive quality. The Insurer shall not be liable under this Policy for the cost of repairing or replacing the specific item of Covered Property that has itself experienced any of the conditions …. However, this exclusion shall not be construed to exclude loss of or damage to other items of Covered Property that is caused by an event resulting from any of the conditions described above ….” (CP § IV.D.)")
    P(d, "The Letter’s conclusion — that damage “to adjacent structures and systems, while not themselves corroded, is nonetheless damage ‘resulting from’ corrosion” — is the precise construction the policy says the exclusion “shall not be construed” to bear. Coupled with § II.C (each tank, pipe rack, electrical system and building is “a separate item of Covered Property”) and the Ensuing Loss Provision, § IV.D excludes only the cost to repair or replace Tank 7.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Concession and open item.** Absent other coverage, Greenfield should expect the Tank 7 repair/replacement cost to be excluded. The Equipment Breakdown Enhancement Endorsement (PNN-CP-END-006) may provide coverage for sudden breakdown of tanks or vessels notwithstanding § IV.D; the full endorsement must be obtained. The Acadian estimate should isolate the Tank 7 line items. Lost MDEA inventory is a separate item of Covered Property (stock) that did not itself corrode; its loss by release implicates § IV.J and the Sudden and Accidental exception rather than § IV.D.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Assessment:** Strong only as to Tank 7 itself; no basis as to all other property.", align="j")

    H(d, "D. Faulty Maintenance Exclusion, § IV.E (Letter § IV.D)", 2)
    P(d, "**The Letter quotes only the first clause.** The full exclusion defines “faulty or inadequate maintenance” as “the failure to perform maintenance activities that are customary and usual for the type of property involved, in accordance with applicable industry standards and the manufacturer’s recommendations,” judged by “the maintenance practices prevailing at the time,” and provides that it “does not apply if the Named Insured demonstrates that it maintained the Covered Property in accordance with applicable industry standards … and the loss or damage was not proximately caused by a failure of maintenance.” The Letter applies none of these standards.", align="j")
    P(d, "**The record satisfies the safe harbor, and Pinnacle’s own expert says so.**", align="j")
    B(d, [
        "API 653 is “the recognized industry standard” for above-ground storage tank integrity (Vector § 4.4). Greenfield’s program was “structured in accordance with API 653”; external inspections were “at regular intervals consistent with API 653 requirements” (24-month cycle: 2021, 2023, next June 2025); and the internal inspection interval (2019 → ~2029) was calculated from measured corrosion rates (CTIS 2023 § 1; CMMS § 1).",
        "API 653 does not require an internal inspection based on minor external surface corrosion; such a finding “is a maintenance condition to be addressed through protective coating repair and monitoring, which is the action that Greenfield undertook” (Vector § 4.4). CTIS itself made “[n]o recommendation … for internal inspection” and found no condition “that would require advancement of the next scheduled internal inspection” (CTIS 2023 § 6).",
        "Greenfield completed the recommended recoat on August 3, 2023, within the 90-day window, conducted monthly operator rounds, and performed annual CP surveys (CMMS 2.4–2.11).",
        "Vector “did not identify any specific deficiency in Greenfield’s inspection or maintenance practices that would constitute a departure from recognized industry standards” (Concl. 8).",
        "Proximate cause is also absent: the internal corrosion “was not visible or detectable through routine external inspection methods” (Concl. 5), and no internal inspection was due.",
    ])
    P(d, "**The Letter’s factual premises are wrong.** It states that Greenfield “did not take adequate steps to investigate or remediate” (it recoated within 60 days of the report); that the 2023 report identified corrosion at “the precise location where the catastrophic failure occurred” (Vector: different surface, mechanism, and severity); that a two-year interval to the next external inspection was a failure (it was the API 653 cycle CTIS recommended); and, in its fact summary, that the corrosion was “exacerbated by inadequate cathodic protection” (Vector makes no such finding; all CP readings were within NACE SP0169 criteria; and CP protects only the external soil-side tank bottom, not the internal shell-to-annular weld — CTIS 2023 § 4.7). Inferring inadequate maintenance from the severity of the corrosion alone is a res ipsa argument the exclusion’s definition does not permit.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Risks to manage.** Pinnacle may retain a different expert to argue that, because MIC and amine SCC are “well-documented degradation mechanisms in carbon steel equipment exposed to amine solutions” (Vector § 4.2), a prudent operator in amine service would have used a shorter, risk-based internal inspection interval; that the 2019 internal inspection data did not justify a 10-year interval; or that the October 2024 SE-quadrant CP reading at −0.85 V signaled a corrosion problem. Greenfield should obtain the full 2019 internal inspection report (CTIS-2019-0314-GF07) and retain an independent API 653/metallurgy expert now. Even if the exclusion applied, it is subject to the Ensuing Loss Provision and would not reach fire damage.", align="j")
    P(d, "**Assessment:** Weak.", align="j")

    H(d, "E. Late Notice (Letter § IV.E)", 2)
    P(d, "**The Letter conflates notice with proof of loss.** It quotes the 60-day notice requirement but then measures compliance by the date of the “formal proof of loss” (April 10, 2025, day 27). The CP Policy treats these as “separate and distinct requirements with separate deadlines” (§ V.A): notice “as soon as practicable, but in no event later than sixty (60) days,” which “may be given by telephone, electronic mail, or in writing” (§ V.A(a)); and a sworn proof of loss “within ninety (90) days after the date of loss” (§ V.A(d)).", align="j")
    B(d, [
        "**Notice:** given in writing by email to Pinnacle’s claims address at 11:00 a.m. on March 14, 2025, roughly nine hours after the loss, containing every element § V.A(a) requires (date, description, Covered Location). Pinnacle acknowledged “receipt of the notice of loss” on March 15, opened the claim under both policies, and assigned an examiner.",
